title: The Great Kurultai on the Onon: Temüjin becomes Chinggis Khan
place: Headwaters of the Onon River, Khentii, Mongolia
summary: In 1206 an assembly of the steppe peoples at the source of the Onon raised a white standard and proclaimed Temüjin Chinggis Khan, and his followers were reorganised into units of a thousand.
detail: After two decades of feuds, betrayals and victories over Tatars, Kereits and Naimans, Temüjin stood unchallenged on the steppe. At the Onon assembly he did not merely take a title; he rebuilt steppe society. The old tribes were broken up and re-sorted into ninety-five units of a thousand (mingghan) under loyal commanders, many of them men of humble birth such as Jebe and Subutai. His personal guard, the keshig, grew to ten thousand and became both an elite reserve and a school for administrators. His adopted brother Shigi Qutuqu was made chief judge, recording verdicts in the Uyghur script. Loyalty, not lineage, was now the road to power, and the whole nation was organised for war.
significance: Created the unified, decimally organised war-state that would conquer from Korea to Hungary.
uncertaintyNote: The year is secure across the Secret History, Juvaini, Rashid al-Din and the Yuanshi. The assembly is placed only at the Onon's headwaters, so it is drawn as a region, not a point. The number and names of the mingghan commanders vary between sources, and the origin of the title Chinggis is debated.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §202 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.125-126)

title: Jochi's campaign to the Forest Peoples
place: Siberian forest belt, from Lake Khövsgöl to the upper Yenisei

sides.opponent: Oirat, Buryat, Kirghiz and other Forest Peoples

summary: Chinggis sent his eldest son Jochi north-west into the taiga, where the Oirat, Buryat, Barqun, Ursut, Qabqanas, Qangqas, Tubas and Kirghiz submitted, mostly without fighting.
detail: The Secret History dates the expedition to the year of the hare, 1207. Quduqa Beki of the Oirat came over first and guided Jochi into the forests. One after another the hunting peoples of the taiga came in, and the Kirghiz lords of the upper Yenisei offered white gyrfalcons, white geldings and black sables in token of submission. Jochi returned with their chiefs, and marriage alliances bound the Oirat ruling house to Chinggis's family. The gains were more than furs: the northern flank was secured, and the Kirghiz country offered grain and iron. The peace was fragile. The Tümed rose in 1217, killing the general Boroqul, and had to be subdued again.
significance: Secured the Mongols' northern flank and its resources before the great wars to the south.
uncertaintyNote: The Secret History gives 1207; Rashid al-Din and the Yuanshi date some Kirghiz submissions to 1208. The route is not recorded, and the peoples' territories are not mapped as polygons, so the event is drawn as a broad region.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §239 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.154-155)

title: Destruction of the last Merkit force near the Chu River

sides.opponent: Merkit remnants under the sons of Toqto'a Beki

summary: Mongol forces under Subutai hunted down the Merkits who had fled west under the sons of Toqto'a Beki and destroyed them near the Chu River.
detail: The Merkits had been Chinggis's enemies since they carried off his wife Börte. After their chief Toqto'a Beki was killed on the Irtysh in the winter of 1208–09, his sons fled west with the survivors. The Secret History tells how Chinggis ordered Subutai to follow them wherever they went, even if they flew into the sky like birds or dived under the earth like marmots, and it mentions carts with iron-rimmed wheels for the long pursuit. Subutai caught them near the Chu River and destroyed them. The campaign carried Mongol arms toward the frontiers of Qara Khitai and, eventually, of the Khwarazmian Empire.
significance: Ended the Merkits as a people in arms and pulled Mongol power westward toward Central Asia.
uncertaintyNote: The chronology is disputed. The pack row dates the event after 1206 and before 1211, following the Secret History's ordering, and Juvaini notes variant 1205 and 1208 dates for the preceding Irtysh fight. Against this, the Yuanshi biography of Subutai places his final destruction of the Merkits in 1217, and many modern historians follow that date. The river identification (Chu, or the 'Chem' of other sources) is uncertain, so the event is drawn as a region.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §236 (de Rachewiltz translation p.153)

title: The Uyghur idiqut submits to Chinggis Khan
place: Uyghur kingdom of Qocho and Besh-Baliq, Turfan region

opponent: Barchuq Art Tegin, idiqut of the Uyghurs

summary: The Uyghur ruler Barchuq threw off Qara Khitai overlordship by killing its resident commissioner, sent envoys offering allegiance to Chinggis, and later came to court in person to pay homage.
detail: In 1209 the idiqut Barchuq Art Tegin had the Qara Khitai overseer in his kingdom killed, then sent envoys east. Chinggis welcomed the offer; Barchuq came in person, most sources say in 1211, bringing gold, silver, pearls and silks, and was promised a Chinggisid princess and honoured as a fifth son. The bargain served both sides. The Uyghurs kept their kingdom, while the Mongols gained a literate, commercial and multilingual Turkic elite. Uyghur scribes, the Uyghur script, and Uyghur administrators and merchants became the backbone of the early empire's chancery and finances, and Uyghur troops marched in later Mongol campaigns.
significance: The first settled state to submit peacefully, supplying the empire's script and many of its administrators.
uncertaintyNote: The repudiation of Qara Khitai is dated 1209 (some accounts 1208); Barchuq's personal audience is usually dated 1211. The submissions of the Qarluq ruler of Qayaligh and of Almaliq were separate and are not part of this event. The event concerns the polity at Qocho and Besh-Baliq, not a single point.

title: Capture of Wulahai, gateway to Western Xia
place: Wulahai (Uraqai), northern frontier of Western Xia
summary: The frontier fortress of Wulahai, guarding the road from the Gobi into the Tangut kingdom, fell to the Mongols during their Western Xia campaigns: first in 1207, and again in 1209 after the defeat of a Xia field army.
detail: Western Xia, a Buddhist Tangut kingdom astride the great bend of the Yellow River, was the weakest of Mongolia's settled neighbours and a natural testing ground. After a plundering raid in 1205, Chinggis returned in 1207 and took Wulahai, but his army could not hold what it captured and withdrew. In 1209 he came back in greater force. Xia sent the crown prince Li Chengzhen against him; the Tangut army was beaten, its deputy commander Gao Lianghui was captured, and Wulahai fell again. From there the road lay open toward the Helan mountains and the Tangut capital, Zhongxing.
significance: Opened the Mongols' first sustained war against a settled state, a rehearsal for the war on Jin.
uncertaintyNote: The pack row's id says 1209 but its date label says 1207. The Yuanshi (juan 1) records a capture of Wulahai in the 1207 campaign and another in the 1209 campaign after the Xia field army's defeat; the Shengwu qinzheng lu likewise records the renewed campaign, and Wang Guowei's note reconciles its dating against the Yuan sources. This event therefore spans 1207–1209. Wulahai's modern site is disputed; the marker is a rough placement in the Urad–Langshan area.

title: Siege of Zhongxing and the failed river diversion
place: Zhongxing (modern Yinchuan), capital of Western Xia
summary: Unable to storm the Tangut capital, the Mongols tried to turn river water against it; the embankment broke, the water escaped outward, and the siege was lifted before Xia negotiated its submission.
detail: After breaking through the Helan mountain passes, where the Tangut general Weiming Linggong was lured out by a feigned retreat and captured, the Mongols reached Zhongxing in 1209. Its walls were beyond their siegecraft, so they tried engineering: a dike to divert river water against the city. Around the turn of 1210 the embankment gave way and the water poured outward instead, and the besiegers had to pull back. Yet the Tangut court's nerve had gone. Its appeal to Jin for help had been refused, and Emperor Xiangzong sought terms. His submission is the subject of the next event.
significance: Revealed the limits of early Mongol siegecraft, but still pushed Western Xia toward submission and left Jin exposed.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi (juan 1) gives the sequence: approach to Zhongxing, attempted inundation, embankment failure with water flowing outward, withdrawal, and negotiated submission. How far the city itself was flooded, and the layout of the works, are not reconstructed here. Some later accounts say the water flooded the Mongol camp; the primary wording supports only that it escaped outward.

title: Western Xia submits and pays tribute in camels
summary: The Tangut ruler became Chinggis Khan's vassal, gave him a daughter in marriage, and pledged tribute of camels, woollens and falcons, promising to serve as the khan's right hand.
detail: The Secret History has the Tangut ruler declare that his people would be the khan's right hand. He promised camels raised in the grass of his country, woollen cloth and trained falcons, and gave Chinggis his daughter, known as Chaqa, as a wife. His refusal, a decade later, to send troops for the western war would prove fatal. For the moment the arrangement suited both sides. Xia kept its throne and its territory; the Mongols gained a supply base and a secure flank for the war against Jin, which began in 1211. The episode also exposed Jin's diplomacy: it had refused to help Xia, reasoning that it profited when its enemies fought each other.
significance: Made Western Xia a tributary and removed Jin's western buffer on the eve of the Jin war.
uncertaintyNote: The pack row follows the Secret History's year of the sheep (1211). The Yuanshi and most modern chronologies put the submission at the end of the 1209 campaign, in early 1210. Both dates are plausible readings of compressed sources; this event keeps the 1211 label. No location is asserted, so the kingdom is drawn as a region.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §§249-250 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.167-168)
Yuanshi, ch. 1 (Taizu benji)

title: Renewed siege of the Tangut capital; the ruler flees to Xiliang
place: Zhongxing (Yinchuan), royal city of Western Xia
summary: Mongol forces again besieged the Western Xia royal city; Emperor Shenzong withdrew to Xiliang, leaving the defence to others, then submitted, and the besiegers withdrew.
detail: Relations had soured since 1210. Xia had turned to war with Jin but resented Mongol demands, and in 1217 Mongol forces returned to the Tangut heartland and laid siege to Zhongxing. Rather than stay in his capital, Emperor Shenzong went west to Xiliang (Liangzhou) and delegated the defence. The pressure worked: Xia again offered submission, and the Mongols withdrew. The respite was brief. Two years later the Tangut court refused Chinggis's demand for troops for the war in Central Asia, and that refusal would lead to the final campaign of 1226–27.
significance: Reasserted Mongol overlordship over Xia just before the western war, without resolving Tangut resentment.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi places the siege in its 13th year (1218); the Xixia ji (juan 27) discusses the conflict and prefers 1217 because Jin reports knew of the siege by January 1218. The pack adopts 1217. The Mongol commander is not clearly named.

title: The Tanguts refuse troops for the western war
summary: When Chinggis asked his Tangut vassal to send troops for the war against Khwarazm, the Tangut court refused, and the minister Asha Gambu answered with open mockery.
detail: Chinggis reminded the Tanguts of their promise to be his right hand. Before the ruler could reply, according to the Secret History, the powerful minister Asha Gambu scoffed that if Chinggis lacked the strength to fight, he had no business being khan. No troops came. Chinggis, with the Khwarazm war about to begin, postponed his revenge, but he did not forget. When he renewed war on Xia in 1226 he cited the refusal and the insult, and the Secret History presents the final destruction of the Tangut state as punishment for both.
significance: Broke the Mongol–Xia alliance and supplied the justification for the final Tangut war.
uncertaintyNote: Known mainly from the Secret History, which recalls the refusal retrospectively when narrating the 1226 campaign. The mocking words are attributed to Asha Gambu, not to the ruler. As a diplomatic event it has no point location; it is drawn as a region around the Xia court.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §265 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.185-187)
Dunnell, The Great State of White and High

title: The final Tangut campaign opens: Asha Gambu defeated in the Alashan
place: Alashan region, west of the Helan Mountains
summary: Chinggis Khan launched his last war to punish Western Xia, defeating Asha Gambu in the Alashan and pressing operations against every Tangut force that resisted.
detail: The campaign began badly for the khan. While hunting wild asses at Arbuqa, the Secret History says, his horse reared and threw him, and he ran a fever. His family urged him to go home and return later; he refused, sending envoys instead. When Asha Gambu answered with another taunt, inviting the Mongols to come and fight in the Alashan, Chinggis marched. Asha Gambu was defeated and captured, and the Mongols pursued his men into the mountains. Chinese records describe a wider offensive in 1226: Khara-Khoto, Suzhou, Ganzhou and Liangzhou fell one after another along the Hexi corridor, some massacred, some spared.
significance: Began the war that would end the Tangut state within eighteen months.
uncertaintyNote: The pack row supports the campaign opening and the Alashan battle from the Secret History, not the precise sequence of city captures in Chinese sources, which is mentioned here only as context. The timing of the riding accident (winter 1225–26 or 1226–27) is disputed. No battle point or route is drawn.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §§265-266 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.185-187)
Yuanshi, ch. 1 (Taizu benji)

title: Lingzhou: defeat of the Tangut relief army
place: Lingzhou (near modern Wuzhong), on the Yellow River
summary: As the Mongols attacked Lingzhou, south of the Tangut capital, Western Xia sent its last great field army under Weiming Linggong to relieve it; Chinggis crossed the river and destroyed it.
detail: By late 1226 the Mongols had swung east from the Hexi corridor and invested Lingzhou, a key city on the Yellow River guarding the southern approach to Zhongxing. Weiming Linggong, a veteran Tangut commander, led a large relief army. Chinggis crossed the river to meet it, and the Xia army was routed. The victory is recorded both in the imperial annals and in the biography of Chaghan, a Tangut-born officer raised in Chinggis's household who fought in the campaign. Lingzhou fell, and nothing now stood between the Mongols and the capital. Later tradition adds that Yelü Chucai took only books and rhubarb from the plunder.
significance: Destroyed Western Xia's last field army and sealed the kingdom's fate.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi dates the attack to the 11th lunar month (roughly December 1226; the pack gives November). The exact crossing point, the battlefield and the forces involved are not known; Chinese figures for the Xia army (up to 300,000) are not credible. The Yelü Chucai anecdote comes from his later biography.

title: The last Tangut ruler submits and is executed: end of Western Xia
place: Western Xia heartland, around Zhongxing and the Liupan Mountains

opponent: Li Xian (Iluqu Burqan), last Xia ruler

casualties: Great loss of life among the Tangut population and elite; no reliable figure
summary: Besieged and cut off, the last Tangut ruler came to submit with gifts; he was put to death on Chinggis Khan's orders, and the Tangut state was destroyed.
detail: Through 1227 the Tangut capital held out while Chinggis, weakened since his fall from a horse, spent the summer in the cooler hills to the south. At last the ruler, whom the Secret History calls Iluqu Burqan, came before the khan bearing gifts including golden images of the Buddha, vessels of gold and silver, boys and girls, geldings and camels. He was received outside the door of the khan's tent, renamed, and executed. The Secret History has Chinggis order the Tanguts wiped out and give their wealth to his wife Yisüi. The khan himself died that same year, in the midst of this campaign. The Tangut people survived under Mongol rule, but their state was gone.
significance: The first complete destruction of a state by the Mongols, and Chinggis Khan's final act.
uncertaintyNote: The pack row removes a precise place claim: where the ruler surrendered is uncertain. The order of the submission, execution and Chinggis's death is ambiguous; Chinese and Persian sources say the ruler's death was kept secret until after the khan died. The extent of the massacre is debated.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §§267-268 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.187-189)

title: Invasion of Jin: the northern passes and the Juyong gorge
place: Northern passes of Jin: Yehuling, Huanerzui and the Juyong Pass

strength.opponent: Chinese sources speak of hundreds of thousands, an implausible figure; certainly larger than the Mongol army

summary: In 1211 Chinggis crossed the Gobi, shattered the Jin armies guarding the northern passes at Yehuling and Huanerzui, and took the Juyong Pass, the last barrier before the capital.
detail: The Önggüd, keepers of the Jin frontier walls, opened the way. The Jin commanders spread their army along the ridges of Yehuling, the Wild Fox Ridge. Their envoy, the Khitan officer Shimo Ming'an, defected and revealed their dispositions. Muqali charged up the slope into the Jin centre with Chinggis following, and the broken Jin army was cut down as it fled through the Huanerzui (Badger Mouth) defile. The Secret History says the dead lay piled like rotten logs. Jebe then took the walled Juyong gorge by feigning retreat, drawing the garrison into the open before turning on it. The Mongols reached the outskirts of Zhongdu.
significance: Destroyed Jin's northern field army and opened north China to two decades of Mongol conquest.
uncertaintyNote: The Secret History narrates a single pass campaign; the pack merges the separately labelled Yehuling battle (sometimes dated February 1212) into this event. Chinese sources date Yehuling to the autumn of 1211 and describe it more fully. Battle sites on the ridge are reconstructed, so the event is drawn as a pass corridor. All army sizes are uncertain.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §247 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.165-166)
Yuanshi, ch. 1 (Taizu benji) and ch. 119 (biography of Muqali)

title: First siege of Zhongdu and the Jin settlement: a princess and tribute
summary: With the Mongols before the walls of Zhongdu, the Jin court submitted, sending Chinggis a princess, gold, silk, horses and attendants, and the Mongol army withdrew.
detail: Zhongdu's triple walls and towers were beyond Mongol siegecraft, and the besiegers were suffering from disease. Some Jin officers urged an attack on them; the court chose to pay. The Secret History tells how the Jin ruler sent a princess as bride for Chinggis, with gold, silver, satins and goods as much as the army could carry, and the Mongols lifted the siege and went back north through the passes. Chinese sources name the princess Qiguo, a daughter of the murdered emperor Wanyan Yongji, and add 500 boys and girls and 3,000 horses. Neither side treated the arrangement as more than a pause.
significance: A humiliating payoff that bought Jin only weeks before the court fled the north.
uncertaintyNote: Date conflict. The pack row follows the Secret History, which places this settlement inside its 1211 campaign narrative, and removes a 1214 date. But the Yuanshi and Jinshi date the princess-and-tribute settlement firmly to spring 1214, after the 1213–14 campaigns; the Mongols had approached Zhongdu in 1211–12 but withdrew without a settlement. This event therefore spans 1211 to April 1214; the settlement itself belongs at the end of that span.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §§248-250 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.166-168)

title: Through the Zijing Pass: the Juyong defence turned
summary: When Jin re-fortified the Juyong Pass, Mongol forces went around it by the Zijing route to the south-west, putting the Jin defenders under pressure from front and rear.
detail: By 1213 Jin had closed the Juyong gorge again, reportedly with iron-sheathed gates and caltrops scattered across the approaches. Rather than batter at it, Chinggis left a screen facing the pass and led the main army south-west through the Zijing pass, one of the gates in the Taihang barrier. Once through, the Mongols could strike the Juyong defenders from behind and fan out onto the north China plain. The Jin history, looking back, contrasts the effort spent on holding Juyong with the Mongol movement by Zijing that left Jin forces caught between two fronts, and it records later Jin attempts to organise the Zijing pass defences.
significance: A classic Mongol turning movement that opened the north China plain for the 1213–14 campaigns.
uncertaintyNote: The Jinshi (juan 102–103) supports the manoeuvre at pass level only; the exact crossing, route and any battle are not reconstructed. The date is circa 1213. Details of the Juyong fortifications come from the Yuanshi and Rashid al-Din.

title: Qasar's eastern column and the submission of the Jin capital Beiging
place: Liaoyang (Jin Eastern Capital) and the Liaoxi corridor
summary: During the 1213–14 campaigns Chinggis's brother Qasar led the left wing east along the coast, bringing the Jin capital the Secret History calls Beiging into submission and subjugating towns on the way back.
detail: In the winter of 1213–14 Chinggis split his army into three wings. While his sons swept Shanxi and he himself drove down the plain toward Shandong, Qasar took the left wing east along the Bohai coast into Liaoxi and the Jurchen homeland. The Secret History says Beiging submitted to him and that he subjugated the towns along his return route. The Eastern Capital, Liaoyang, had already fallen once, to Jebe in the winter of 1212–13, when he feigned a retreat and then rode back to storm the unguarded city. Mongol control in the north-east long remained contested between Jin loyalists, the Khitan rebel Yelü Liuge and the Jurchen warlord Puxian Wannu.
significance: Extended Mongol operations into the Jurchen dynasty's north-eastern homeland.
uncertaintyNote: The pack row identifies the Secret History's Beiging as the Jin Eastern Capital (Liaoyang), and the marker follows it. However, Beiging is more usually read as Beijing, the Jin Northern Capital (Dading, near modern Ningcheng), which Chinese sources say surrendered to Muqali in 1215; Liaoyang had been taken earlier by Jebe. The date is a circa range.

title: The Jin court abandons Zhongdu; Chinggis renews the war
summary: Weeks after the settlement, Emperor Xuanzong left Zhongdu for Nanjing (Kaifeng); Chinggis treated this as a breach, renewed the war, defeated the Jin forces sent against him, and closed in on the abandoned capital.
detail: The Jin court had been in turmoil since autumn 1213, when the general Heshilie Zhizhong murdered the emperor and was himself killed by his rival Zhuhu Gaoqi, who had been fighting the Mongols north of the capital. In the summer of 1214 the new emperor, Xuanzong, moved south to Nanjing behind the Yellow River. To Chinggis the move proved Jin meant to fight on. On the road south, Khitan auxiliary troops mutinied and went over to the Mongols, bringing a ready-made army back toward Zhongdu. Mongol and allied forces defeated the Jin troops in the passes and began a blockade of the capital that lasted into 1215.
significance: Jin abandoned the north, giving the Mongols both a pretext and new allies for taking Zhongdu.
uncertaintyNote: The Secret History (§251) compresses the renewal, the pass battle and the imperial flight; the pack merges Zhuhu Gaoqi's October 1213 fighting north of the capital into this event. Dates of the court's departure (summer 1214) vary by weeks between sources. No city capture is claimed here; see the 1215 occupation.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §251 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.168-169)

title: Occupation of Zhongdu
summary: Abandoned by its emperor and starved by blockade, Zhongdu passed into Mongol hands in 1215; Chinggis sent officers to inventory its treasuries, and one of them, Shigi Qutuqu, refused the Jin officials' gifts.
detail: After the court's flight, the capital's defenders held out through the winter of 1214–15 while relief columns carrying grain were intercepted. In late spring 1215 the commander Wanyan Chenghui took his own life and his colleague fled south, and the city passed to the Mongols and their Khitan allies. Plunder and fire followed, and a visiting Khwarazmian embassy later described a scene of devastation. The Secret History dwells on another moment: Chinggis sent Önggür, Arqai Qasar and Shigi Qutuqu to take stock of the gold, silver and silks. The keeper offered them presents; Shigi Qutuqu refused, saying the city now belonged to the khan, and was praised for it. Among the captives was the Khitan scholar Yelü Chucai.
significance: The first great imperial capital to pass to the Mongols; the metropolis of north China became a Mongol base.
uncertaintyNote: The pack treats this as a control transfer after the court's flight rather than a battle. Chinese sources date the surrender to late May or early June 1215. Accounts of the burning and killing (including Juzjani's report of Khwarazmian envoys) are vivid but cannot be quantified.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §252 (de Rachewiltz translation pp.169-170)

title: Muqali takes command in north China
place: North China south of the Taihang: Hebei, Shandong and Shanxi

strength.focus: Rashid al-Din: about 23,000 Mongols plus larger Khitan, Jurchen-defector and Chinese contingents

summary: Turning west, Chinggis made Muqali Prince of State with command of the war south of the Taihang; Muqali set up a field administration at Yun and Yan and campaigned through Daming, Shandong and Taiyuan in 1217–18.
detail: Muqali received the title Taishi Guo Wang and a standard of nine white tails, with orders that his commands be obeyed as the khan's own. With a small Mongol core he could not garrison every city, so he recruited Chinese commanders such as Shi Tianze and Zhang Rou, whose private armies became hereditary Mongol commands, and learned to spare cities that surrendered. From his headquarters at Yun and Yan he struck through Hebei, taking Daming, then into Shandong, and in 1218 into Shanxi, where Taiyuan fell. He would campaign on until his death in 1223, never breaking Jin's defensive line along the Yellow River.
significance: Established the Mongol method of ruling north China through local Chinese commanders.
uncertaintyNote: Yuanshi juan 119 dates the appointment to the 8th lunar month of 1217 (August–September; the pack says August). The markers are named cities in his dated campaigns, not a route or conquered surface. Troop totals differ between Rashid al-Din and the Yuanshi.
sources: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%85%83%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7119
https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E9%87%91%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B714
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Franke and Twitchett (eds.), Cambridge History of China vol. 6

title: Jebe ends Qara Khitai: flight and death of Küchlüg
summary: Chinggis sent Jebe against the Naiman prince Küchlüg, ruler of Qara Khitai; Küchlüg fled from Kashgar and was captured and killed near the Badakhshan frontier.
detail: Küchlüg had fled west after the Naiman defeat, usurped the throne of the Qara Khitai Gür-khan, and turned on his Muslim subjects in Kashgar and Khotan, banning public worship; Juvaini says he had an imam crucified on the door of his madrasa. When Jebe advanced, he announced that everyone might keep their own religion. Townspeople rose and killed Küchlüg's soldiers billeted in their homes. Küchlüg fled south-west into the mountains toward Badakhshan, where he was run down, captured and beheaded. According to Juvaini, Jebe then sent Chinggis a hundred chestnut horses with white muzzles, recalling the horse he had once shot from under the khan.
significance: Brought the Mongol frontier to the borders of the Khwarazmian Empire.
uncertaintyNote: Juvaini is the main narrative; the Secret History is brief. The place of capture is uncertain (often put in the Sariqol valley), so the pursuit is drawn as a corridor region. The pursuit may have run into 1219.
sources: Secret History of the Mongols §237 (de Rachewiltz translation p.153)
Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, pp.66-68
Biran, The Empire of the Qara Khitai in Eurasian History
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion

title: First clash with the Khwarazm-shah, between the Qaili and Qaimich
place: Qipchaq steppe, north of the Syr Darya (river identifications uncertain)
summary: Campaigning in the steppe, Sultan Muhammad overtook a Mongol force that was pursuing Qangli and Qipchaq fugitives; a day-long battle ended with no clear victor, and the Mongols slipped away.
detail: The Mongols were hunting fugitives in the steppe and, by their own account, had no orders to fight the sultan. Muhammad attacked anyway. Juvaini tells how the Mongol wings pressed hard, nearly reaching the sultan's centre, until his son Jalal al-Din restored the line. The fighting lasted until nightfall. The Mongols then lit fires across their camp and withdrew in the dark. The Yuan history's biography of Subutai records the same indecisive clash in its own terms. The encounter left a deep impression: Juvaini says that Muhammad, having seen the Mongols' courage, grew fearful of them, and his later strategy of dispersing his army into garrisons may reflect that fear.
significance: Gave both sides a first measure of each other before full war, and shaped the sultan's defensive strategy.
uncertaintyNote: Juvaini places the fight between rivers he calls Qaili and Qaimich, which cannot be securely identified; the Yuanshi calls the place Hui-li. His editor notes rival chronologies of 1216 and 1219. Juvaini names Jochi as commander, while the Yuanshi credits Subutai; neither the Irgiz location nor Jochi's command is asserted here.
sources: https://archive.org/stream/historyoftheworl011648mbp/historyoftheworl011648mbp_djvu.txt
https://archive.org/details/historyoftheworl011648mbp
Yuanshi, ch. 121 (biography of Subutai)
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion

title: The Otrar incident: a Mongol caravan killed
summary: The governor of Otrar arrested a trade caravan sponsored by Chinggis and his nobles; with Sultan Muhammad's approval its merchants were killed and their goods seized, and a Mongol embassy sent to seek redress failed.
detail: Chinggis had just proposed a trade agreement to Muhammad. The caravan, mostly Muslim merchants financed by Mongol princes and nobles, reached Otrar laden with silver, silk and furs. Governor Inalchuq, a kinsman of the sultan's mother, denounced them as spies and, with Muhammad's sanction, had them put to death and their goods sold. A single camel-driver escaped to carry the news. Chinggis sent envoys demanding that the governor be handed over; Muhammad had the leading envoy killed and the others humiliated. Juvaini says Chinggis went alone up a mountain and prayed for three days before declaring war.
significance: The direct cause of the Mongol invasion of Central Asia and the Islamic world.
uncertaintyNote: The caravan's size is not part of the canonical claim; Juvaini gives about 450 merchants, other sources differ. Whether some merchants really were spies is debated, as are the details of the embassy (Nasawi and Ibn al-Athir give different accounts).
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, pp.77-81 (Boyle trans.)
Secret History of the Mongols §254 (de Rachewiltz translation p.171)
Nasawi, Sirat al-Sultan Jalal al-Din
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion

title: Siege of Otrar and the invasion divides

strength.focus: Whole invasion army: modern estimates 100,000–150,000; chronicle claims far higher

summary: The Mongols struck first at the city whose governor had provoked the war; Chagatai and Ögedei besieged it while other columns branched down the Syr Darya and toward Bukhara, and after about five months the city and then its citadel fell.
detail: Arriving in autumn 1219, Chinggis divided his army: Chagatai and Ögedei stayed to besiege Otrar, Jochi went down the Syr Darya, a detachment went upstream toward Banakat and Khujand, and Chinggis himself with Tolui struck across the desert toward Bukhara. At Otrar the commander Qaracha lost heart and tried to slip out with his men, but was caught and executed by the Mongols for deserting his master. The town fell; Inalchuq fought on in the citadel for another month, his men reduced to throwing bricks. Taken alive, he was put to death. A later story that molten silver was poured into his eyes and ears is not in the earliest sources.
significance: Opened the war by punishing its instigator, while Mongol columns fanned out across Transoxiana.
uncertaintyNote: Juvaini gives a five-month siege plus a month for the citadel, so the event spans 1219–1220; exact dates vary by weeks. The molten-silver execution is a later legend. No siege works are reconstructed.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, pp.81-86 (Boyle trans.)
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion

title: Capture of Bukhara

opponent: Kök Khan and other Turkish commanders

casualties: Citadel garrison killed; townspeople plundered and many conscripted; fire destroyed much of the city. No reliable totals
summary: Chinggis appeared out of the Kyzylkum desert behind the Khwarazmian lines; Bukhara's town surrendered, but its citadel resisted and was stormed and destroyed.
detail: Instead of attacking the Syr Darya line, Chinggis led his central army across the Kyzylkum, taking Zarnuq and Nur on the way, and appeared at Bukhara in February 1220. The Turkish troops tried to break out at night and were cut down near the Amu Darya. The town's notables then opened the gates. The citadel held out until captives filled its moat and it was stormed, and its defenders were killed. Juvaini describes Chinggis riding into the great mosque, and then addressing the notables from the pulpit of the festival prayer ground as a punishment sent by God for their sins. The townspeople were driven out, the city plundered and burned, and young men taken to serve in the siege of Samarkand.
significance: A strategic masterstroke that split the Khwarazmian defences and panicked the empire.
uncertaintyNote: Usually dated February 1220 (Barthold). Juvaini distinguishes the town's surrender from the citadel's resistance. Chinggis's speech is reported by Juvaini, writing in the 1250s in Mongol service, and should be read as literary.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, pp.102-108 (Boyle trans.)
Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion
May, The Mongol Conquests in World History

title: Capture of Samarkand
summary: After fighting outside the walls, Samarkand's leaders surrendered; the Mongols took the city and overcame the last resistance in the citadel.
detail: The capital of Transoxiana had a strong Turkish garrison and war elephants, and Sultan Muhammad had expected it to hold for years. Chinggis paraded masses of Bukharan captives before the walls, organised in tens like soldiers, to magnify his apparent strength. A sortie was driven back with heavy losses. The Qangli Turkish troops, kinsmen of the queen-mother, then negotiated their own surrender, hoping to join the Mongols; instead they were separated from the population and killed. The clerics and notables opened the gates, and the citadel's last defenders were overcome. Thousands of craftsmen were shared out among Mongol princes and taken east. Muhammad abandoned Transoxiana and fled.
significance: Ended organised Khwarazmian resistance north of the Amu Darya.
uncertaintyNote: Barthold dates the surrender to about mid-March 1220; the exact day is not asserted. Garrison sizes given by Juvaini and Nasawi are inflated and are not carried forward.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, pp.116-122 (Boyle trans.)
Nasawi, Sirat al-Sultan Jalal al-Din
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion

title: Storm of Termez
summary: Termez refused to surrender; after an eleven-day siege the Mongols stormed it and killed its people.
detail: After summering in the hills near Nasaf, Chinggis moved south to the Amu Darya. Termez, a fortified town on the river's north bank, refused his summons, trusting in its walls and the river. The Mongols set up mangonels and battered it for eleven days before storming it. Juvaini tells a grim story of an old woman who begged for her life by saying she had swallowed a great pearl; she was cut open, and the khan then ordered all the dead searched. From Termez the Mongols prepared to cross into Khorasan and Tokharistan, and the road to Balkh lay open.
significance: Opened the crossing of the Amu Darya into Khorasan and Afghanistan.
uncertaintyNote: Juvaini places Termez before Balkh in a 1220–21 sequence; the pack uses 1220 as the working year (usually autumn). The pearl anecdote may be a traveller's tale.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, pp.128-130 (Boyle trans.)
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion

title: Jebe and Subutai hunt Sultan Muhammad across Iran
summary: Chinggis sent Jebe and Subutai after the fleeing sultan; they chased him through Khorasan and northern Iran, while Balkh submitted and received a Mongol governor. Muhammad died a fugitive on a Caspian island.
detail: With orders to take the sultan dead or alive, the two generals crossed the Amu Darya. Balkh submitted to them and was given a governor; other towns that opened their gates were spared, those that resisted were attacked. Muhammad fled from Nishapur to Qazvin and on into western Iran, his escort shrinking at every stage, and the Mongols more than once nearly caught him. At last he crossed to a small island off the Caspian shore of Mazandaran, where he died of illness, destitute, around the turn of 1221, having named Jalal al-Din as his heir. Meanwhile his mother and harem were taken in a Mazandaran fortress.
significance: Destroyed the Khwarazmian state's central authority; resistance passed to Jalal al-Din.
uncertaintyNote: The consulted passage supports the pursuit and Balkh's initial submission, not a single capture of Balkh or the family's capture as one event. The sultan's death is dated December 1220 to early 1221, and the island is probably Ashur Ada. The pursuit is drawn as a region, not a route.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, ch.XXV pp.142ff. (Boyle trans.)
Nasawi, Sirat al-Sultan Jalal al-Din
Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion

title: Defeat of the Georgian royal army on the Xunan plain
place: Xunan (Khunan) plain, Georgian–Armenian borderlands on the Kura
summary: Subutai's force entered the Georgian–Armenian borderlands in the winter of 1220–21 and destroyed King Lasha's army on the Xunan plain with a feigned retreat and ambush.
detail: After wintering on the Mughan steppe, the raiders rode north-west into the Kura valley. Georgia was at the height of its power and preparing to join a crusade against Egypt. Its royal army, under Giorgi IV Lasha and his great commander Ivane Mkhargrdzeli, met the Mongols on the Xunan plain. The Armenian chronicler Kirakos describes the stratagem: the Mongols fell back, the Georgian cavalry pursued, and a hidden force struck them from ambush. The royal army was routed with heavy losses and the king was wounded. Queen Rusudan later wrote to the Pope that the invasion had wrecked Georgia's crusading plans, giving Latin Europe some of its first news of the Mongols.
significance: Broke Georgian military power at its height and brought first, confused news of the Mongols to Latin Europe.
uncertaintyNote: Kirakos places the battle in 1220/21; the pack corrects an earlier 1222 date. Georgian chronicles, Kirakos and Ibn al-Athir count two or three separate Georgian defeats in 1221–22 and disagree on their order; a second defeat in 1222 is not part of this event. Xunan's site is only approximately known, so it is drawn as a region.
sources: Kirakos Gandzakets’i, History of the Armenians ch.11 (Bedrosian trans.)
Kartlis Tskhovreba (Georgian Chronicles)
Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
Jackson, The Mongols and the West

title: Capture of Merv
casualties: Very heavy; the chronicle totals (Juvaini 1,300,000; Ibn al-Athir 700,000) are not credible and no reliable figure exists
summary: Tolui's Khorasan army reached Merv, one of the great cities of the Islamic world; after a failed sortie and negotiations the governor surrendered, and most of the population was put to death.
detail: Merv was crowded with refugees and had defied an earlier Mongol reconnaissance. Tolui arrived in February 1221 and rode round the walls for days, studying the defences. The defenders' sortie was driven back. Governor Mujir al-Mulk then accepted terms and came out with gifts. The Mongols ordered the population onto the plain, set aside some four hundred craftsmen and a number of children, and divided the rest among the troops to be killed. Juvaini says a local sayyid spent thirteen days counting the dead, though his totals cannot be believed. The city's famous libraries and the oasis irrigation suffered lasting damage.
significance: The emblematic atrocity of the Khorasan campaign and a lasting blow to its urban life.
uncertaintyNote: The capture is certain. The casualty totals and the chroniclers' language of total annihilation are not part of the canonical claim; the chronicle numbers far exceed any plausible population. Dates vary within late February to early March 1221.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, “Of Merv and the Fate Thereof,” pp.151ff. (Boyle trans.)
Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion
Morgan, The Mongols

title: Battle of Parwan: Jalal al-Din defeats Shigi Qutuqu
place: Parwan region, north of Kabul (near modern Charikar)
summary: Jalal al-Din's coalition of Turkish, Khalaj and Afghan troops defeated the Mongol army sent against him near Parwan, the first major Mongol defeat of the war.
detail: The new sultan had gathered an army at Ghazni. Chinggis's adopted brother Shigi Qutuqu, chief judge of the empire, met him near Parwan. The Mongols tried to magnify their numbers by setting felt dummies on their spare horses, but Jalal al-Din held his ground by having his men dismount and fight on foot. Then his cavalry charged and broke the Mongols, who fled with heavy losses. Chinggis is said to have taken the news calmly, remarking that Shigi had grown too used to victory. The triumph quickly fell apart: Jalal al-Din's commanders quarrelled over a captured horse, and the Afghan and Qangli contingents rode away.
significance: Proved the Mongols could be beaten, inspiring revolts in Khorasan and bringing Chinggis south in person.
uncertaintyNote: Juvaini names the defeat as the trigger for Chinggis's rapid pursuit, but its date (spring to early autumn 1221) is disputed and the battlefield is not fixed, so it is drawn as a region. Army sizes (Juvaini gives the Mongols 30,000–45,000) are uncertain, and the battle details come mainly from sources sympathetic to Jalal al-Din.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, ch.XXII pp.133-134 (Boyle trans.)
Nasawi, Sirat al-Sultan Jalal al-Din
Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion

title: Capture of Bamiyan and the death of a grandson of Chinggis
summary: Mongol forces took Bamiyan after stiff resistance; during the siege a grandson of Chinggis was killed by an arrow, and the town was destroyed in reprisal.
detail: Bamiyan's fortress guarded the passes between Balkh and Ghazni in the valley of the giant Buddhas. During the siege a grandson of Chinggis, named by Juvaini and Rashid al-Din as Chagatai's son Mö'etüken, was shot and killed. The khan ordered that no captives be taken and no plunder collected, and the town was destroyed. The sources tell how he broke the news to Chagatai only after making him swear not to weep or complain. Local tradition later called the hilltop ruins Shahr-i Ghulghula, the city of screams. The Buddhas themselves survived until 2001, when the Taliban destroyed them.
significance: A byword for Mongol vengeance on those who killed a member of the ruling family.
uncertaintyNote: The capture and the royal death are supported; the prince's identity varies in some sources, and Juvaini's account of total extermination is not part of the canonical claim. Timing within 1221 (before or after Parwan) is uncertain. The name Shahr-i Ghulghula may postdate the event.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, pp.131-133 (Boyle trans.)
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh
Barthold, Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion

title: Battle of the Indus
place: West bank of the Indus, perhaps near Dinkot/Kalabagh (disputed)

strength.opponent: Probably smaller after the desertions following Parwan

summary: Chinggis caught Jalal al-Din with his back to the Indus and destroyed his army; the sultan escaped by riding his horse off the high bank into the river and crossing to the far side.
detail: Chinggis marched from Ghazni at a punishing pace and caught the sultan before boats could carry his army across. Jalal al-Din fought from dawn, charging the Mongol centre again and again, but the Mongols closed in around him and a detachment worked round his flank. When all was lost he took a fresh horse, threw off his armour and plunged from the bank into the river, swimming to the far shore. Chinggis stopped his archers from shooting and, according to Juvaini, told his sons that such a man was the kind of son a father should wish for. The sultan's army was destroyed behind him, and his family drowned.
significance: Destroyed the last Khwarazmian field army, though Jalal al-Din lived on as a wandering warlord for a decade.
uncertaintyNote: The traditional date of 24 November 1221 is widely repeated but not certain; the event is dated to the month. The battlefield is disputed between points near Dinkot/Kalabagh and farther north near Nilab/Attock, so it is drawn as a region with no point. Army sizes are estimates.
sources: Juvayni, History of the World-Conqueror I, ch.XXII pp.133-135 (Boyle trans.)
Nasawi, Sirat al-Sultan Jalal al-Din
Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri
Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate

title: Beyond Derbent: the Alans, Circassians and Cumans defeated
place: North Caucasus and the Cuman (Qipchaq) steppe
summary: Passing beyond Derbent into the lands of the Alans and Lakz and then the Qipchaq steppe, the Mongols defeated the Alans, Circassians and many Cumans, whose survivors fled to the Rus' for help.
detail: Having stormed Shamakhi, the Mongols forced guides from the Shirvanshah to lead them around the great fortress of Derbent through the mountains. Beyond it they faced Alans and Cumans in alliance. Ibn al-Athir tells how the Mongols persuaded the Cumans to stand aside, appealing to their shared Turkish kinship and sending them part of the plunder; they then beat the Alans and afterwards fell on the scattered Cumans. The Rus' chronicle adds that the Tatars had defeated Alans, Circassians and many Cumans, killing the khans Yuri Konchakovich and Daniil Kobyakovich. Survivors under Köten fled west to his son-in-law Mstislav of Galich and begged the Rus' princes for aid.
significance: Opened the western steppe to the Mongols and drew the Rus' princes into the war.
uncertaintyNote: Ibn al-Athir supplies the Derbent passage and the divide-and-rule stratagem; the Rus' chronicle supplies the defeated peoples and Cuman names. No battle site (including the Kuban once suggested) or route is fixed, so the campaign is drawn as a region. It ends before the Kalka campaign of mid-1223.
sources: https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/source/1220al-Athir-mongols.asp
https://www.drevne.ru/lib/kalka.htm
Fennell, The Crisis of Medieval Russia 1200–1304
Jackson, The Mongols and the West

title: First Mongol seizure of Sudak
summary: After the North Caucasus and Cuman campaign, Mongol raiders reached the Black Sea port of Sudak, seized the city and scattered its inhabitants.
detail: Sudak was the great emporium of the Crimea, where Qipchaq slaves, furs and steppe goods met Byzantine and Italian merchants. Ibn al-Athir reports that the Mongols came to it after defeating the Cumans, took it, and that its people dispersed, some fleeing into the mountains and some crossing the sea to Anatolia. A marginal note in a Greek service book from Sugdeia records that the Tatars first came on 27 January 1223. The raid showed how far the Mongol horsemen had ranged, and it disrupted a commercial hub whose fate would matter to the Mongol economy of the western steppe in later decades.
significance: The Mongols' first appearance on the Black Sea coast, striking a key hub of Mediterranean–steppe trade.
uncertaintyNote: The day comes from the Sugdeia Synaxarion marginal note; Ibn al-Athir independently reports the seizure without a date. The approach route, siege details and any wider Crimean conquest are not reconstructed.
sources: https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/o-date-podchineniya-gotii-tataro-mongolam
https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/source/1220al-Athir-mongols.asp
Jackson, The Mongols and the West

title: Battle of the Kalka River
place: Kalka River (probably the Kalchik or Kalmius), near the Sea of Azov

strength.opponent: Estimates of 30,000–80,000 Rus' and Cumans; chronicle numbers unreliable

casualties: The Novgorod First Chronicle says only one in ten survived; several princes and many boyars killed
summary: A Rus'–Cuman coalition crossed the Kalka after pursuing a retreating Mongol force and was destroyed piecemeal over several days; the Prince of Kiev, who surrendered, was crushed to death under the victors' feasting platform.
detail: Persuaded by Köten, the southern princes gathered at Kiev and marched down the Dnieper. They killed Mongol envoys and chased a Mongol rearguard for days, feeling victorious. At the Kalka, Mstislav of Galich crossed with the Cumans without waiting for Mstislav of Kiev, whose men stayed fortified on a hill. The Mongols turned. The Cumans broke and fled back through the Rus' ranks, and the Galicians and Chernigovites were cut down. The Kievans held their camp for three days, then surrendered on a promise that no blood would be shed. The prisoners were laid under boards on which the Mongol commanders feasted, and suffocated.
significance: The first Mongol clash with the Rus', a warning ignored until Batu's invasion fifteen years later.
uncertaintyNote: The Novgorod First Chronicle (under A.M. 6732) gives 31 May; other Rus' texts give 16 June. The river is usually identified with the Kalchik or Kalmius, but the battlefield is unknown, so it is drawn as a river corridor.
sources: Novgorod First Chronicle, Synodal Text, A.M. 6732 (Michell & Forbes trans., 1914, pp.64-67)
Hypatian Chronicle
Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
Fennell, The Crisis of Medieval Russia 1200–1304

title: The Volga Bulgars ambush the returning Mongols
summary: Heading home after the Kalka, the Mongol detachment entered Volga Bulgar territory, where the Bulgars ambushed it at several places and defeated it; the survivors withdrew toward Saqsin.
detail: Ibn al-Athir reports that when the Mongols came to Bulgar at the end of the Islamic year 620, the Bulgars laid ambushes in several places, drew them on, then fell on them from behind, killing many. The survivors turned back toward Saqsin on the lower Volga and made their way east through the steppe to rejoin the armies of Jochi and Chinggis. Later tradition embroidered the story, but whatever its scale, the defeat ended the great raid. Volga Bulgaria was marked for vengeance: it was among the targets named for the 1229 dispatch against the west, and in 1236 it fell to Batu and Subutai.
significance: One of the few Mongol defeats of the period, and a grievance that shaped later western campaigns.
uncertaintyNote: Attested chiefly by Ibn al-Athir; Rus' chronicles are silent. The Islamic year 620 ended in January 1224, giving a late 1223 to early 1224 date. No battlefield (including the Samara bend often cited) and no survivor count is asserted; the event is drawn as a region.
sources: https://www.vostlit.info/Texts/rus/Athir_3/text1.phtml?id=12570
https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/source/1220al-Athir-mongols.asp
Jackson, The Mongols and the West
May, The Mongol Conquests in World History

title: Siege of Kangdong and the Goryeo–Mongol brotherhood compact
summary: Mongol and Goryeo forces jointly besieged Khitan rebels holed up at Kangdong fortress; afterwards the Mongol commanders asked that the two states remain brothers, and a tribute relationship began.
detail: Khitan rebels, driven out of Manchuria by the Mongols and their allies, had fled into Korea and seized Kangdong. In the winter of 1218–19 a Mongol force under Qachi'un and Jala, with Eastern Xia auxiliaries, arrived in pursuit, and the Goryeo general Kim Chwi-ryeo joined them with troops and supplies. The Khitans surrendered early in 1219. The Mongol commanders then proposed that Mongols and Koreans be brothers forever, and the Yuan history records a Mongol envoy's demand for annual tribute. It was an alliance, not a surrender, but Mongol envoys' growing demands soured it, and the murder of an envoy in 1225 would become the pretext for invasion.
significance: The first Goryeo–Mongol relationship, whose breakdown led to the invasions from 1231.
uncertaintyNote: The pack treats this as a diplomatic-military turn, not Goryeo's submission. Dates follow the Goryeosa's lunar calendar. No meeting point or siege works are reconstructed; the event is anchored to the Kangdong area.
sources: https://db.history.go.kr/goryeo/itemLevelKrList.do?parentId=kr_103r_0010_0020&types=r
https://zh.wikisource.org/zh-hant/%E5%85%83%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7208
Henthorn, Korea: The Mongol Invasions

title: Ögedei sends Kökedei and Subutai against the Qipchaqs, Saqsin and Bulghar
place: Qipchaq steppe, Saqsin and the Volga Bulghar region
summary: At his accession Ögedei dispatched Kökedei and Subutai westward against the Qipchaqs, Saqsin and the Volga Bulghars, reopening the western front.
detail: Ögedei's election in 1229 was followed at once by orders for campaigns on several fronts: Chormaqan to Iran, the renewed war on Jin, and a western army. Rashid al-Din records that Kökedei and Subutai were sent with a force against the Qipchaqs, Saqsin on the lower Volga and Bulghar. Subutai knew this ground from the great raid of 1220–23, and Volga Bulgaria had defeated him on the way home. The dispatch did not achieve a decisive conquest; the steppe peoples and the Bulgars held out, and a much larger effort would be needed. That effort came in 1236, when the western princes' campaign under Batu, with Subutai again in command, finally overwhelmed them.
significance: Restarted Mongol operations in the western steppe and set up the great western campaign of 1236.
uncertaintyNote: Rashid al-Din is the main source; the course of the fighting in 1229–35 is poorly documented. No outpost attacks, route or front are asserted, and the target area is drawn as a broad region.

title: Chormaqan's western campaign brings the Transcaucasus under Mongol rule

sides.opponent: Khwarazmian remnants, Georgia, Armenian princes and local rulers

summary: Ögedei sent Chormaqan west with about 30,000 men; over the 1230s his army broke Jalal al-Din, occupied north-western Iran and brought Georgia and Armenia under Mongol military authority.
detail: Chormaqan, a former keshig quiver-bearer, crossed Khorasan in 1230 and burst into Azerbaijan in the winter of 1230–31, scattering Jalal al-Din's forces. He then made the Mughan steppe his base, a perfect pasture for Mongol horses. Cities that submitted, such as Tabriz, were spared; those that resisted, such as Ganja, were stormed. From about 1236 his commanders moved into Georgia and Armenia, taking fortress after fortress, and Queen Rusudan fled to Kutaisi. The Secret History sums up his achievement briefly as the subjection of the western peoples and the stationing of garrisons among them. By the end of the decade the Transcaucasus lay under Mongol military government.
significance: Established permanent Mongol rule in the Transcaucasus and the base from which the Ilkhanate later grew.
uncertaintyNote: The pack row dates the campaign to the 1230s and supports only the high-level subjection and garrisoning; the precise completion date in Georgia and Armenia (c. 1236–39) is not asserted. No territorial polygon is drawn.

title: Jin holds the Tong Pass: victories at Dachangyuan and Daohuigu
summary: Holding the Tong Pass and the line of the Yellow River, Jin generals Wanyan Heda and Yila Pua checked repeated Mongol attacks, with victories at Dachangyuan and Daohuigu.
detail: After Chinggis's death the Jin rallied. Their field army under Wanyan Heda and Yila Pua guarded the Tong Pass, the narrow gate between the Wei valley and the Yellow River plain, and struck out against Mongol forces that came too close. At Dachangyuan the officer Wanyan Chen Heshang, leading a few hundred men of the elite Loyal and Filial army, routed a far larger Mongol force. At Daohuigu, in early 1231, the Jin again drove back a Mongol attack in which Subutai was involved; Ögedei is said to have rebuked him. These were Jin's last great successes, and they persuaded the Mongols that the pass could not be forced head-on.
significance: Jin's last successful defence, which pushed the Mongols to outflank the pass through Song territory.
uncertaintyNote: The Jinshi (juan 112–113) records the repeated victories in these years. Most chronologies date Dachangyuan to early 1228, before the 1230–31 label, while Daohuigu falls in early 1231. The Dachangyuan marker is approximate (Ningxian area, Gansu); Daohuigu's location is too uncertain to mark. No pass line or battle footprint is drawn.

title: Siege and fall of Fengxiang
summary: Tolui attacked the Jin stronghold of Fengxiang in 1230; after an early setback and imperial reinforcement, the siege dragged into 1231 and the city fell in April.
detail: Fengxiang was the key to the Wei valley west of the Tong Pass and a base from which Jin could threaten Mongol-held Shaanxi. In 1230 Tolui moved against it and met an initial check; Ögedei sent reinforcements. The Jin field army nearby, wary of leaving the Tong Pass, would not come to its relief in force. The siege continued through the winter, and in the spring of 1231 the city fell. Its capture gave the Mongols the western Wei valley and the starting point for the great outflanking march, led by Tolui, through Song territory toward the Jin heartland in Henan.
significance: Cleared the way for Tolui's flanking march around the Tong Pass defences.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi (Tolui's biography) dates the attack to 1230; the Jinshi records the siege continuing in January 1231 and the fall in April. The pack corrects an earlier single-year label. No siege works are reconstructed.

title: End of Jalal al-Din
place: Country of Amid (Diyarbakır region), south-eastern Anatolia
summary: A Mongol pursuit destroyed Jalal al-Din's remaining force in the country of Amid; the sultan escaped alone into the mountains, where he was reported killed by Kurds.
detail: After the Indus, Jalal al-Din had carved out a realm in western Iran and Azerbaijan, sacked Tbilisi and made enemies of all his neighbours; in 1230 the Seljuks and Ayyubids defeated him at Yassıçemen. When Chormaqan's army arrived that winter, the sultan fled west. Mongol horsemen caught his camp in the country of Amid and scattered his men. He escaped alone into the nearby mountains. His biographer Nasawi and later chroniclers report that he was killed there by a Kurd, some say in revenge for a brother slain by the Khwarazmians. Rumours that he survived as a wandering dervish circulated for years. His leaderless troops became mercenaries and, in 1244, sacked Jerusalem.
significance: Ended the last Khwarazmian resistance and opened the Transcaucasus and eastern Anatolia to the Mongols.
uncertaintyNote: Bar Hebraeus and Ibn al-Athir report the pursuit and the death, while also preserving the survival story; the death report is therefore qualified. Nasawi dates it to mid-Shawwal 628 (about mid-August 1231). No death point or pursuit route is drawn.

title: First Mongol invasion of Goryeo and the negotiated withdrawal
place: North-western Goryeo, from the Yalu to the capital Kaegyŏng
summary: Citing the murder of a Mongol envoy in 1225, Sartai invaded Goryeo in 1231, attacked districts that would not submit and camped at Anbuk; the court negotiated peace, accepted Mongol overseers, and the army withdrew early in 1232.
detail: Sartai crossed the Yalu in autumn 1231 and took many northern towns, setting up his headquarters at Anbuk. Some places fought hard: at Guju the commander Pak Sŏ held out for months against catapults, scaling ladders and fire, a defence that impressed the Mongols themselves. Other columns advanced toward the capital, Kaegyŏng. The military ruler Choe U chose to negotiate. Goryeo sent tribute and accepted Mongol resident overseers (darughachi) in the north-western districts, and Sartai withdrew early in 1232. The settlement did not last: within months Choe U took the court to Ganghwa Island and the war resumed.
significance: Began nearly three decades of Mongol invasions of Korea.
uncertaintyNote: The Goryeosa annals and Yuanshi juan 208 agree on the invasion, negotiations, overseers and withdrawal. A later Yuan claim that seventy-two overseers were killed is not treated as established. Dates convert approximately from lunar months. No invasion route is drawn; Anbuk and the capital are the anchors.

title: Ögedei's final Jin campaign: Tolui's flanking march and Sanfengshan
place: Henan and the southern approaches to Kaifeng

strength.opponent: The last Jin field army; Chinese figures of 150,000 are not reliable

summary: In 1231 Ögedei renewed the war on Jin; while he pressed the Yellow River line, Tolui marched around the Tong Pass through Song territory, and early in 1232 the Jin field army was destroyed at Sanfengshan.
detail: Carrying out a plan attributed to Chinggis on his deathbed, Tolui led a column south from the Wei valley through Song Sichuan and Shaanxi, down the Han River, and into Henan behind the Jin defences. Wanyan Heda turned the Jin army back to meet him, harried day and night by Mongol horsemen who refused battle. Near Sanfengshan, in a snowstorm that lasted for days, the starving, frozen Jin troops were surrounded as Ögedei's forces arrived from the north. The Mongols left a gap to encourage flight, then cut down the fleeing army. Heda was killed and Chen Heshang, captured, died defying his captors. Kaifeng now lay defenceless.
significance: Destroyed Jin's last field army and doomed the dynasty.
uncertaintyNote: The Secret History (§§271–273) supports the renewed campaign and the destruction of Jin at a general level; the Sanfengshan details come from the Jinshi and Yuanshi. The battle is dated to the first lunar month of 1232 (about February). No battle point or route line is drawn.

title: Siege of Kaifeng: plague, thunder-crash bombs and surrender
casualties: Heavy losses to epidemic and famine; the Jinshi's claim of some 900,000 coffins in fifty days is a chronicle figure
summary: Subutai besieged the Jin capital; the defenders used gunpowder bombs and fire lances, but after epidemic, broken negotiations and the emperor's flight, the officer Cui Li surrendered the city in 1233.
detail: The assault began in spring 1232. The Mongols threw up a siege wall and battered the city with catapults. The defenders answered with some of the earliest recorded gunpowder weapons: the thunder-crash bomb, an iron-cased charge lowered on chains to blast Mongol sappers in their cowhide shelters, and flying fire lances. Negotiations brought a pause, then collapsed after Mongol envoys were killed. In summer an epidemic swept the crowded city. Emperor Aizong slipped out at the start of 1233 to seek refuge elsewhere. In the capital the commander Cui Li seized power and surrendered to Subutai. Yelü Chucai persuaded Ögedei to spare the population rather than massacre it.
significance: Brought down the Jin capital and is a landmark in the history of gunpowder warfare.
uncertaintyNote: The pack row gives March 1232 (assault), January 1233 (surrender) and April 1233 (Mongol entry). These are lunar months in the Jinshi and Yuanshi; converted, they fall roughly in April 1232, February 1233 and May 1233, which this event uses. The epidemic's nature and toll are debated, and descriptions of the bombs are read differently by historians of technology.

title: Cheoin Fortress: Sartai killed
place: Cheoin Fortress (near modern Yongin), south of the Han River
summary: During the second Mongol invasion of Goryeo, the commander Sartai attacked the small fortress of Cheoin and was killed by an arrow; his leaderless army withdrew.
detail: In the summer of 1232 the military ruler Choe U moved the king and court to Ganghwa Island, trusting the tidal strait to stop horsemen, and ordered the population into mountain fortresses and islands. Sartai returned in the autumn and ravaged the peninsula south of the capital. At Cheoin, a modest walled post south of the Han River, the defenders included a Buddhist monk, Kim Yun-hu, who had taken refuge there. When Sartai led an attack on the fortress he was struck by an arrow and killed; Korean tradition credits Kim Yun-hu with the shot, and he later refused the reward. Without their commander, the Mongols withdrew.
significance: A rare killing of a Mongol commander in the field, ending the second invasion of Korea.
uncertaintyNote: The Goryeosa biography of Kim Yun-hu and Yuanshi juan 208 agree on the attack and Sartai's death from an arrow. The date is the 12th lunar month of 1232 (December 1232 to January 1233). The attribution of the shot to Kim Yun-hu is Korean. No combat point or approach route is drawn.

title: End of the Jin dynasty
summary: The final Jin campaign ended in early 1234 with the destruction of the last Jin ruler; Mongol garrisons and commissioners were installed in the conquered cities.
detail: Aizong had fled Kaifeng with a small following and ended up at Caizhou in southern Henan. The Song court, seeing a chance to avenge the loss of north China a century earlier, sent troops and grain to help the Mongols. The city starved through the winter of 1233–34. According to the Chinese histories, as the walls fell in February 1234 Aizong passed the throne to a kinsman and took his own life, and the new ruler died in the fighting the same day. The Secret History records simply that the Jin ruler was destroyed and that Mongol garrison commanders and officials were placed in the cities. North China was now Mongol, and only Song lay to the south.
significance: Completed the conquest of north China and removed the buffer between the Mongols and Song.
uncertaintyNote: The pack row follows the Secret History's high-level account of dynastic destruction and control; the Caizhou abdication sequence (dated 9 February 1234 in the Jinshi) is context rather than part of the canonical claim, and the terminal location is shown as a region.
